utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around are the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to first welcome the accused. I would like to greet also the counsel. I'd like to welcome Mr. Stringer, Ms. West, their assistants, and all the people who are here to help us. We are 25 minutes behind schedule as there was a technical problem which has now been solved. I would now like to give the floor to the registrar who I think has two IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has submitted its response to documents tendered by 1D and 3D via witness Neven Tomic. This list shall be given Exhibit number IC 00895 and IC 00896 respectively. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Registrar. Madam West you have the floor. You have one hour and 45 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of your report? Why don't you get that out. Thank you. Now you have, in your direct testimony, spoken about the 1991 census of which you were a part; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that when the interviewers went out to collect the information from the residents, this was a face-to-face interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the interview method that is used.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. You described situations in your testimony where people were reluctant to give their JMBGs. What is the source of your information for that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that people were reluctant. I said that some people provide their IDs, some didn't. Some went to work without leaving their ID and you obtain information from household members who are at home. One household member can provide data for all the other members of the household. Very often, even in the 1991 census, companies would issue everybody with certificates -- certificates as to where they worked, what their IDs were, what was the name of their professional activity, but it doesn't mean that everybody had it on them. There was a recommendation for everybody to leave these pieces of paper at home so as to enable their household members to provide correct data, but I don't know whether everybody complied with that. On the certificates that the employees of various companies were issues, the key issue was the ID of the company that you worked in and the line of profession that the company was involved in, because those questions were something that people did not answer to readily, and statistics found that key information for the analysis of the economic structures in the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But you anticipated my next question which regarded the people who were employed, and so is it your testimony that if a person was employed the company would actually provide a certificate with their JMBG that they were supposed to give to the interviewer?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not like you say. The companies were supposed to issue every employee in their hand. It was not submitted to their home address. Primarily, this certificate contained the ID of the company and the industry that the company belonged to, but I'm not sure whether those contain the IDs of the citizens themselves. I'm not sure. The forms still exist and I could check. The purpose of these certificates, or the primary purpose, was not to provide the ID of the individual citizens but the IDs of the companies and the industries that the companies were a part of. The issuing of these certificates by the companies would have been pointless if it was done only to provide the citizens ID, because in 1991 every citizen in the former Yugoslavia had their own ID either on their identification document or their driving licence or their social security card. So it was not the primary goal of such certificates issued by companies to provide citizens with IDs. I'm not disputing the fact that the form may have contained that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came to the OTP in April of this year, you had access to the OSCE voter registry database; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go into close session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if this exhibit could be taken off of e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, you've given extensive testimony regarding the OSC [sic] voter registry. Are you familiar with the eligible requirements?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what OSCE required, the OSCE requirements?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we may have P 10735. That's in the second binder as well. That is page 2 of the English, page 69 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you look right in front of you, you'll see it. So this is the general framework agreement for -- it's the Dayton peace agreement regarding elections. It's what Dayton required. And if you go to page 2 of the English, Article IV talks about eligibility, and I'm just going to read that. It says: "Any citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina aged 18 or older whose name appears on the 1991 census for Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be eligible in accordance with electoral rules and regulations to vote. A citizen who no longer lives in the municipality in which he or she resided in 1991 shall, as a general rule, be expected to vote in person or by absentee ballot in that municipality, provided that the person is determined to have been registered in that municipality as confirmed by the local election commission and the provisional election commission. Such a citizen may, however, apply to the commission to cast his or her ballot elsewhere. The exercise of the refugee's right to vote shall be interpreted as confirmation of his or her intention to return to BiH. "By election day ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "By election day, the return of refugees should already been under way, thus allowing many to participate in person in elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The commission may provide an electoral rules and regulations for citizens not listed in the 1991 census to vote." So you would agree, Professor, that according to this Article IV, in order to be eligible to vote per OSCE, you just had to be on the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They to be citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina; they had to be of age, over 18; and it was recommended for them to be on the census, but that was not the absolute requirement. If they were not on the census, citizens could bring two witnesses who themselves were on the census, and prove that both that they were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that they could vote. Not only two witnesses, they could go to their religious leader. If you want me to, I can provide the OSCE instruction to see what precedents were made. I -- one of the recommendations were that the citizens were on the 1991 census; but if they were not, they could prove that they were citizens. Would you like me to show you the recommendation?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, Professor. I don't disagree with you on that, but I would like to go back to this language under Article IV. And, here, it also talks about something we were previously talked about, which is where their vote should count, the choice as to where they want their vote to count. Do you see that in here?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you. Citizens could vote wherever they wanted to vote, providing that was approve by the commission, if there was something in dispute. If they were in the same municipality in 1991 where they wanted to cast their vote in 1996, then they did not have to go to the commission at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Professor, would you agree with me that where a person wanted their vote to count is very different from where they actually walked into an office and registered to vote?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. First, I have to go to an office and declare my wish. On the assumption that I was in Mostar and that I was currently in Sarajevo for any reason, either voluntarily or forcibly, and when elections are announced, it would be only logical for me to go to Sarajevo, and I can say, "I would like to have my vote counted in Mostar. If not, then I express my wish to vote in Sarajevo." Then they will say, "Yes, prove since when you have been in Sarajevo. Did you arrive in 1996 or after 1996?" I have to be a declared permanent resident or I have to have a refugee status, and I have to have a document proving that I was a refugee who was not able to go back to their original place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think we agree on this point, because as you just explained, this person would want their vote to count in Mostar, but they actually registered to vote in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not always like that, I'm saying. That may be approved. I may have my vote counted in Mostar, but I have to have a good reason, an explanation. If I had moved out voluntarily, I don't want to go back to Mostar, I'm a resident of Sarajevo. If my resettlement was forcible, then I can apply to have my vote count in the place where I resided in 1991; but in the meantime, I could have changed my mind. I'm a refugee of Sarajevo, but that's where I want to stay. There are all sorts of possibilities which I can explain before the commission and the commission may grant approval or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think we're very clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's move to Exhibit 10738, 10738. We'll look at the -- page 7 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is the OSC [sic] adjudication manual. This is the manual that OSCE gave out to the people who worked for them and who worked for the registration to help the employees understand what to do. Now, particularly on page 4 of the English and then page -- excuse me, page 7 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, it talks about in-person registration, and this talks about in-person registration outside the BiH. I'm going to read this and then we'll talk about it. It says: "The voter registration process in the federation and Croatia will essentially parallel the registration process conducted within the borders of BiH. Voter Registration Committee staff will verify illegibility, and applicants will complete scannable registration forms in person at out-of-country voter registration centres." Professor, my question is: Would you agree that this language which suggests that in the BiH, people actually came to the office to register to vote and the OSCE employee had to verify their eligibility? In other words, people came in person themselves to register to vote?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are voters in SRJ and Croatia. This has nothing whatsoever to do with the procedure that was in place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The voters from SRJ or FRY and Croatia came in person. They could not send somebody in lieu of them, but that don't change anything. Voters from the FRY, and I know that for a fact, who had citizenship of Serbia could -- had to have their passport on them proving that they were also residents of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then they would register to vote.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, again, if we go back to this language, it says that that out-of-country registration that they're describing, and you're right, parallels the registration process conducted in-country. So I ask again --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It says "essentially parallels." There's a difference between "parallels" and "essentially parallels," and I suspect the word "essentially" is there for a particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, if I can ask, Professor, again, would you agree that this suggests that in-country, people had to come in to register?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, they did not have to come in person. I suppose that the majority did come in person; but the way I understand it, they didn't have to come in person. It was recommended. Whether they all came in person or not is a different matter. And when you say that it is essentially something that parallels the other process, it does not have to correspond in temporal terms. The process started -- lasted from October to December. To be very precise, the process of registration lasts for two and a half months --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thanks, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and it was --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to move on I'll ask you to go to P 10737, P 10737.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's binder 2.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you look on the screen, Professor, you'll see it.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is the OSCE citizenship verification subcommission form. So, if we go to Article 17, you'll see that right in front of you, and go to part 3, where it says: "If an individual's name is not found on the 1991 census as adjusted for use in the 14 September 1996 elections during the voter registration period, proof of citizenship in 1991 will require the individual to present ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "... will require the individual to present during the voter registration period either a certificate of citizenship issued prior to 1991 or a receipt issued by the appropriate municipal authority to establish that he or she was recorded as a citizen in one of the official municipal record books prior to the 1991 census. All such receipts shall be subject to verification in accordance with the practices and procedures established under the authority ..." So Professor, this is what you were talking about earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But this is only one part of it. The direct recommendation is something that I will take out from my briefcase, and I will show it to you. Can somebody assist me, please. It says here: "How do you verify the identity of voters, recommendation of what documents may be used."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For technical purposes, it may be good to put it on the ELMO and also to identify what the document is, the title of it. So, Professor --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, can you identify what that document is?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the document that I sent to the Prosecution. It is called the Manual for the Registration of Voters. It's from 1997. It was published by the OSCE. I will read or perhaps somebody else can read. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You can go ahead and read the part to which you refer.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Each person registering must provide identification documents." So I'm not going to read everything. The documents that may be used are list here: Personal ID card, certificate of citizenship, passport, birth certificate, certificate, and so on. "Persons who do not have any of the documents -- identification documents listed above may prove their citizenship by proffering a statement that includes: First name and last name, address at the time of the census, personal ID number, and present current address. The statement must be made in the presence of one of the following: A permanent judge, a cleric, a municipal official, or two persons whose names are on the 1991 census." So one of those persons must be present.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to focus on what you said early on. You said that the documents that may be used are listed here: Personal ID card, certificate of citizenship, passport, birth certificate, certificate, and so on. And, so, would you agree with me that the purpose of them providing something physically, a piece of identification, as according to this OSCE verification says - or it doesn't say, excuse me - is to compare is to the 1991 census, so that the OSCE employee can compare that ID to the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, all the voters list, regardless of whether it's peacetime or wartime, are always made on the basis of the database compiled on the basis of the census, always. Now, if there was a war and if there were movements of population, the census must be the basis, at least in the former Yugoslavia. I don't know about other countries. Now, if we were to set up the voters list in Croatia or for the elections in Serbia, the census is used as the basis, because who can record each and every voter? You, first of all, have to know what the electorate is, and you get this idea of what the electorate is on the basis of the census. How can somebody say that 70 per cent or 30 per cent of the voters turned out for the elections? It is stated on the basis of the voters list that were put together prior to the election, prior to the vote, and those voters lists were put together on the basis of the census. Of course, the voters list must be updated. Persons died and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful. And in this case in the 1997 election, 80 per cent of the electorate came out and registered; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not correct. This is what your expert states, but this is not correct. And if you look at her tables where she says that she matched 42.000 and that the number of -- for the population in 1991, that would be about 60 per cent, that's 60 per cent of --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think you misunderstood my question. My question had to do with how many people came out to register in 1997. Isn't it a fact that 80 per cent of the electorate came out in 1997 and actually registered to vote? I'm not talking about matching.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not a fact. Your expert claims that the voters lists lack between 20 and 40 per cent of the voters. In the Blagojevic response, which I also have here, this is what your expert claims.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, madam. But let's go back to what you said earlier, when you were talking about the electoral rolls being based on the census. Would you agree with me, then, at every OSCE registration office, the OSCE employees had both manual copies, physical copies of the 1991 census, and a computer copy of the 1991 census, in order for them to make sure that the person who walked in the door had been on the census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with the terminology, but it may be a translation issue. Registering -- voters are not registered on the basis of the census. It is based on the individual records. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was the census, and the first instruction to whoever is registering the voters is look for that person in the census, but there is a whole series of problems that one encounters in trying to find persons. There is a special note saying "Attention: Because of the quality of the records for the first name and last name, there might be problems with finding persons. If you do encounter this problem ..." --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think this must be a translation issue, because that wasn't my question. My question was: When somebody registered in 1997, walked into the door, isn't it a fact that OSCE had a copy of the 1991 census there both in hard copy and on a computer? That's my question alone.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had copies in the computer with first name, last name, and so on. So not the entire census, just the first name, last name, and some other characteristics, but they did have it. On the basis of the 1991 census, they were trying there to find the person who came to register. Sometimes they would succeed and sometimes they would fail.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's just then in a general way talk about the process that a person went through when they wanted to register to vote. I'll describe it and you just tell me if you agree. It would be: Step one, a person would go to the office; step two, that person would give their name and give some sort of identification that you describe; step three, the OSCE employee would consult the census, whether on the computer or hard copy, to see if the person standing in front of them matched up with the census; step four, if that person is the same person, then it's a match and they can register; but, step five, if they can't find that person on the census, then there would have to be alternative ways for that person to ensure that they were a citizen in 1991. Would you agree with me generally what I just described was the procedure?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes. But when you say something like that, you infer that the OSCE official managed to find Svetlana Radovanovic with that name. Perhaps, he was unable -- they were unable to find Svetlana Radovanovic because it says "Svelana" or "Sjelana"; but then, based on some other identification markers, they can determine that they actually did find me in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- census. So it is the duty of the official --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. That being the case, is it then fair to conclude that in 1997 or 1998, OSCE was the very first organisation to do a matching of the voters electoral rolls with the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1997 and in 1998 in Bosnia, yes. However, if OSCE had not been there, it was -- if it had been peace, there would be electoral commissions that would do that. It just so happened that it was OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that OSCE, as result, acted as a type of filter for the matching that OTP later did?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a chance, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at examples then. When you came here in April, when you came to OTP, you had access to all the data that -- upon which OTP based their results; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had voters lists, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So, in regard to my question yesterday as to whether a match to the JMBG would be ideal, you said: "It would be the best, most reliable method, but not ideal, provided that the personal ID number is unique and correct. It is unique as the name suggests, but it also needs to be correct. It is the most reliable key for matching, having again a numerical key but of a different kind." I then asked: "Had the OTP used the personal identification key only, and that was the only never they used, would you disagree with the results if it was based on that and just that entirely?" Your answer, Professor, was: "The matching method, now we have a problem with the key. If the personal ID number had been used as the key, and if it had been reliable and correct numbers, then the data would definitely be more reliable." Professor, my question now is: With that testimony in mind, do you recall that the OTP matching technique resulted in 142.204 names that they matched up? They literally matched 142.204? Do you recall that information?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, but they did not use the JMBG but the name, the last name, and so on and so forth. If matching was also done with JMBG as the key, it doesn't say how many matches were found according to that key. I know what -- only what your expert stated. She stated there was matching according to name, last name, and ID number, and so on and so forth. And if that is the case, how many were matched according to the ID number?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would give me some reliability. I could say, okay, this is now a reliable result.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you had the capacity to run this test as well, and what percentage of the 142-plus thousand came from a match from the JMBG, and just the JMBG?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, that was not my task at all. I'm not trying to prove any figures here to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, would your opinion of the OTP report change if you knew that 85 per cent of the 142-plus thousand linked names were matched using just the JMBG?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I doubt that there were so many correct JMBGs in -- of citizens in the eight municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna. It would be a precedent. According to what I know, there were major mistakes all over Bosnia in JMBGs of citizens. If 85 per cent of the JMBGs in the eight municipalities of Herceg-Bosna were correct, which doesn't mean that it has 13 digits, and if 85 per cent of the JMBGs in the census were also correct, I would consider this a very high degree of positive matches.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to look at P 10761, and may we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may be heard for two minutes. on page 36, line 24, Judge Trechsel indicate that I pretended, and I understand that this is perhaps a linguistic issue. I understand Judge Trechsel's English is his second or third of the many languages that he speaks, but I do wish to make sure that the record is rather clear. When I stand up and object, I'm not trying to pretend anything. I make submissions. I make them in good faith. I'm not trying to lie, cheat, or to do anything that is inappropriate. So I just want the record to reflect that. I apologise for raising my voice, but that was the issue that obviously got under my nerve, the issue or suggestion that somehow I was pretending. Again, I want to make sure that you know that I don't pretend. I make submissions. I am a member of a bar. I'm considered an officer of the court. We do have certain ethical obligations, and one of the obligations of a lawyer is to be forthright and honest with the Trial Chamber at all times. So I just want to make sure the record is clear. I can only think that Judge Trechsel was not -- did not mean that somehow I was lying to the Bench. It could be just a terminological issue due to linguistics. That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Mr. Karnavas, 100 per cent. It's a linguistic, intercultural problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. West, you have 42 minutes left, I've been told by the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, you have your report directly in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in your report, on page 26 of the English - it's page 24 of the B/C/S - you note that the sample that OTP used, in it, the share and change of rank of the Muslim and Croat population related to the overall population in 1991 and in 1997 and 1998 have not been significantly affected. My question is: In this regard, are you noting that overall in the area that we're talking about the ethnicity proportions did not change, they about stayed the same?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not I who says that; it's your witness, your expert. In the part of her analysis which I quoted from, she says that this is interesting because there were no visible changes in the ethnic structure. I can pinpoint that part. I can tell you where she says so. I quote her in my report. According to the results provided by your expert and according to the table that I drafted for the total area of Herceg-Bosna, the changes are not visible. Yesterday, or the day before, we discussed the shares, 44.4 and 54.6. If you remember, let's not go over the same grounds again. There are no radical changes in the shares of particular ethnic groups in the overall population of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, Professor, that was the bigger point you were trying to make in that discussion of 22 per cent or 10 per cent. It's that there's no significant change overall; correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I was saying was that your expert used non-demographic indicators in order to represent the change in ethnic structure to be bigger than it was actually as a matter of fact. She claims that a share of Croats rose by 22 per cent. But when you take into account demographic indicators, it is not correct that their share rose by less than 10 per cent. I believe 9.8 per cent. In other words, your expert used indicates -- indicators that referred to the percentual change of the per cent, which means that one figure rose in relation to another figure by 22 per cent based on a non-demographic indicator.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But when we talk about the overall ethnicity of the area, that is not something that distinguishes changes in ethnicity within municipalities, does it not?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be seen as having been done by your expert for every municipality. There are myriads of tables there with myriads of repetitions; however, she never presented an analytical table. It is certain that things differed from one municipality to the next when it comes to the ethnic structure. I must say that these changes were the result of what your experts -- expert believes that are good matched numbers. In statistical terms, the good matched number is beyond comparison with the statistical results of 1995, because in her comparison, your expert is mixing apples or pears or apples and oranges.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you had just indicated that, on line 9 and 10: "It is certain that things differed from one municipality to the next when it came to ethnic structures." Now, let's talk about that. I'm going to ask you to look at P 10752, and we'll put this on Sanction. So it should come up on the screen in front of you. Now, Professor, this is one of the OTP tables that regards exactly what you noted, the certain ethnicity changes within municipalities. I'll ask you this: Isn't it true that in 1991, of the area of which we speak, there were eight municipalities that had a relative majority of an ethnicity and six municipalities where there was an absolute majority; however, by the time of 1997, all 14 of those municipalities had absolute majorities? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this data, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So, when you made statements in your direct testimony regarding the lack of an overall change or overall difference of relative rank of ethnicities, you were not looking at the municipalities individually internally, were you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct, no. I looked at every municipality individually, but the problem is as follows: For the years 1997 and 1998, the data was combined by your expert at her own will, rather than using a proper methodological solution. I provided an analytical table not having any other data, but the combination of your expert, to show that at the general level there were practically no changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you -- I'm sorry, Ms. West. Could you indicate what the course of this table is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the PowerPoint presentation the OTP used in Ewa Tabeau's expert testimony, and it is Annex A1 of the OTP report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It is Tabeau, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure it's in evidence, though, Your Honour. I understand it was rejected by the Trial Chamber. So I may be incorrect, but I'm told this was rejected by the Trial Chamber. So if that is the case, then I would object to this table being used for any further testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll check. We'll check. I can't remember at this stage. Witness, I have one question. I'm a bit lost, I have to say. Take a look at Mostar, Srpski Mostar. In 1991, we have 55.6 per cent of Muslims. In 1997, we have 98.3 per cent of Serbs. Is that really possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is also a key methodological problem. If you calculate in this way, then, yes, it is possible. However, there is a problem which is looking at the data according to the new administrative territorial division. This new administrative division was introduced in 1996 or 1997. It divides the Mostar municipality into eight individual municipalities, and every border between the two of these eight municipalities, in this case, for Dr. Tabeau, means resettlement or a change of ethnic structure. People may have remained in the same place but are now divided by borders. And if you have heterogeneous settlements or heterogeneous-ethnic structure, those are usually concentrated, and one line can move that concentration, and you end up with a new municipality with a totally new composition of the population. What you see here is this Srpski Mostar. This Srpski Mostar, with regard to the entire municipality of Mostar, I believe it represents less than 1 per cent of the total population. Now, if you take into account such a small percentage or such a small figure, and you represent them in figures -- in percentages without presenting absolute figures, then you obviously get a mathematically correct representation which excludes many other elements, which might draw your attention to the fact why this is so. Much more reliable -- reliable information would be obtained if she did it according to the administrative and territorial division that was in place in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] Let's take the example of Mostar-Jug. In 1991, we have 49 per cent of Croats, it seems. Then there's a sharp increase in 1997, up to 96 per cent. But looking at this table, somebody else could wonder when did that sharp increase occur. Was it in 1993 or was it after 1993? For a demographer, can a table provide that type of information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No table of this type can be found in the report. There's no way for you to say this happened in 1993, this happened in 1994, 1995, 1996, 1997, and so on and so forth. Dr. Tabeau did everything for the period between 1991 and 1998; however, she does not offer a single sentence or a single way or a single source of data to establish what was happening between 1991 and 1997 or 1998. She cannot say this happened between 1991 and 1992, this happened between 1992 and 1993. In other words, there's no way, because there are no sources of data that would lend themselves to doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, this table had been rejected by the Trial Chamber, but it may be used, of course, to test the credibility of a witness. Otherwise, yes, indeed, this table had not been admitted. Please proceed, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Ma'am, you just indicated that OTP used what I can term as the post-Dayton municipalities, instead of the 1991 municipalities for the analysis. Isn't it true, ma'am, that OTP is not the only organisation that, when determining returning refugees and displaced peoples, used the post-Dayton municipalities?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is, Who is doing what? Many are using the new administration, but are not using the 1991 administrative division to show what happened in the intervening period. Now the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina uses the new administrative division. But if you are a demographer, if you want to have comparative data and if you want the data to be comparable, then you use those elements that you are certain will yield the result that you need. Your expert turned the 1991 division into the new division. It is very difficult, because you have to take the census circles out, and this is a very complex task. Then something that did not exist, such as Mostar South or Mostar North, you first have to go to the statistical circles, to the original material. As a rule, those are the actual forms. They probably don't exist because they are destroyed after three years. So you have to go to the material that you have in the -- on the magnetic media, storage media. Then you --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let's move on. You spoke yesterday about the War Hospital records, and I'd like to show you P 10752. It will be Sanction as well, and that's P 10752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's the one we just had, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, the document that you have in front of you on Sanction is the one to which I'm referring, and I'll ensure that the record's correct about the exhibit, but it is the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, you personally examined the War Hospital records; right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that I personally did it. I acquainted myself with what this data source looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at page iii of your report, and it's page iii in the B/C/S as well. It says "Work performed," number 1, you talk about your colleagues, and then you say: "In addition, I've personally examined the death registers, about 500 pages ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is too much background noise, so the interpreters cannot hear the speakers.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Again, it's under number 1, and you said: "In addition, I personally examined the death registers, about 500 pages, and the registers of the Mostar War Hospital, number of pages unknown." So again, Professor, do you have a memory of personally examining these records?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall that I examined them, but I did not produce any results from the records. But let me tell you what it means, "personally examine." In order for me to acquaint myself with the data source used by Dr. Tabeau, I went through all the materials, but I did not obtain any results from that. Let me show you what my examination looked like, what it boiled down to. If I may put one document on whatever this machine is called.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, I'd like to move on. I asked you whether you personally examine them. You said, yes. Now you're describing that. I think the Court, unless it wants more testimony on this issue, we should move on. So my next question is: In regard to those records, OTP found that 49 people were killed from gunshots, 214 were killed from shelling, 209 from unknown, and the total being 472. Professor, would you agree with me that OTP produced these numbers from counting? There's no matching going on. They went through records to record who was killed by gunshots, who was killed by shelling. It was actually a counting method.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will agree, but there are persons who were killed in traffic accidents and suicides among those who are listed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This figure is not large, but there are some.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. That was not my question. Professor, I'd like to move on to something that we've talked a little bit about and it's the proportion method, and this is something that you discussed in your report. If you can go to page 11 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is page 12 of the English. Page 11 in the B/C/S, page 12 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You wrote: "We note that the proportion method is not used and has never been used in scientific ..." --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't follow you. I really can't follow you. I don't see where you're reading. If it's at page 11, there's not a single sentence that begins the words "I notice ..." Maybe it's an interpretation thing. It says: "The first procedure boils down to simple arithmetic ..." Is this at the beginning of page 11 in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, go to the paragraph that starts "The second procedure ..." Do you see that? It's the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "We note that the proportion method is not used and has never been used in scientific expert research for population migrations. It was occasionally used in statistics until the 1990s, only in the evaluation and sorting of data about unknown age structure. But upon the United Nations' recommendations, it has been eliminated from expert research because of the unreliability of the results obtained by its application." Professor, what is the source of the UN recommendation? Can you cite me a manual or a handbook?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Before a census is taken, the international organisations and the United Nations that have a population department send to all the countries recommendations that have to be taken into account when a census is taken --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- things that should be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. That's not responsive to my question. My question was: Can you cite me a manual or a handbook? You said, Yes. What is the name of the manual or the handbook?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Recommendations for the Census around the year 2000."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But you did not footnote it in your report, did you not?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I'm not quoting from it. I simply say that in accordance with the recommendations that were in place in 1990s, the distribution method, at least when it came to determining the age brackets of the population, should not be use. So I did not make a direct quotation. Those were just the recommendations, the recommendations that were valid for the former Yugoslavia. I cannot now say whether the same recommendations are in place in the USA or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, that's not what you said. I'm going to read this again. You said: "We note that the proportion method is not used ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "... and has never been used in scientific expert research of population migrations. It was occasionally used in statistics until the 1990s," and then you describe the age structure. Then you say: "But upon the UN recommendations, it has been eliminated," eliminated, "from expert research because of the unreliability of the results obtained by its application." So my question is: Can you give me a cite as to where it's -- how the United Nations, when the United Nations said you shouldn't use it any more?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you. "Recommendations for the Census done around the year 2000." But this does not pertain to the first part that you just read, and that is that it is not known that the proportion method is used in professional and expert research. That's not the UN recommendation. Scientific and expert research --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's go to --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- is guided by professionals, by experts --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's go to P 10758, P 10758. This is the UN handbook on migration, binder 3, but it will come up in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's 10758. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This handbook is from the UN website, and it was downloaded last week. I'd like you to look at B/C/S page 3, and it's the English page 5. This excerpt says: "In addition to household registers, the amount of information ..." --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: One moment, ma'am. There you go. Follow along. "In addition to household registers, the amount of information collected by governments for other purposes may be useful in estimating migration. In the United States, base data on migration streams between States is obtained from tax records. Because a substantial majority of American households file tax forms each year, and because they are required by law to enter their social security numbers and current address, computers are able to match records for adjacent years and count the number of movers (See Wetrogan and Long, 1990). "However, because low-income persons are not required to file tax forms, and because persons entering the labor force or entering the country may not have filed in the previous year, only about 80 per cent of the population are covered by matching tax records for adjacent years. Although migration rates are based only on matched records, when these rates are applied to the total population, it is assumed that the uncovered population moves at the same rate. "Wetrogan and Long, 1990 compared these rates with census and current population survey rates for comparable periods and found the differences were small." Professor, you would agree with me that what this UN handbook is talking about when it says, "Although migration rates are based on only match records when the rates are applied to the total population," specifically in regard to that, that's talking about the distribution or proportion method, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the distribution or the proportion method, but it has nothing to do with the method applied by your expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree with me, Professor, that it would be unusual for the UN to advocate this method on their website if they did not recommend it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the UN is doing has anything to do with the official publication of the data relating to population statistics. I did not deny the proportion method. It exists, it is in use, but a scientific or an expert work, at least to my knowledge - and I'm not familiar with all the literature - explaining the migrations, in particular forcible migrations, never used the proportion or distribution method, for a very simple reason: Because you know in advance what you will get when you apply this method, in particular --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that is not --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if you operate with very small numbers statistically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That is not responsive to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is very responsive because we're dealing with two different situations. One is in the United States, for instance, which is the example, people moving voluntarily. Another one is a situation where you had a war. People moved during and after the war, and there are two different reasons. That's the explanation why the witness is saying one cannot be compared with the other, and she should be entitled to provide a full explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. I think it might be useful in order to clear up this matter which is very important. In the section which my learned friend Ms. West quoted from our expert's paper, it's quite clear that she's speaking about a non-representative sample and about data obtained from a non-representative sample, which are then distributed on a larger set, quite unlike the example that is brought up by Ms. West, which speaks about a representative sample of 80 per cent, which is then distributed to the overall population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, on this issue about the proportion method, the Prosecutor is showing you a document stemming from the United Nations. Apparently, it's used in the United States of America to deal with migratory flows. This is something which is checked by tax forms being filed, in which case you can deduce a number of facts. Now, of course, this document can lead to discussions, but Mr. Karnavas made an objection that one should not confuse between regular migrations and voluntary migrations and forcible migrations; and, therefore, you cannot apply the same method in the case of a forced migration or a voluntary migration. Now, you, madam, who are the expert, what do you think about that? Can method be applied to any type of migration, or should it consider the question of forcible migrations with more precise analysis tools?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The method can be applied to all kinds of migrations. The only question is, What sense does it make? You see here a segment of data which is small, and then on the basis of the proportion that you establish there, you extrapolate onto a larger case. So you have 100 cases, and you extrapolate to 400 cases; 140.000 cases to 200.000 cases, and you considered all of them to be forcible. This is not true, because out of all the cases, regardless of the reliability, you can have both voluntary and forcible migrations, and yet you assume that all of them are forcible and you do the opposite. You do not use a bigger sample numerically speaking, but you use a sample that is smaller and which is highly debatable. You apply the proportion method transposing the results to a sample which is twice the size; and, of course, your results is twice as large. An expert who uses this, who has 10 per cent or 20 per cent of known -- known cases or known facts, and then extrapolates to the 80 per cent of the facts that are not known, knows that she will get a higher figure. We yesterday spoke about 135 causes of death that are known, and then this is extrapolated to 404 cases. So, instead of having 70 people as victims of the shelling, the expert estimates that it's 303 victims of shelling. This is entirely unreliable method for migrations or for any other kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Professor, I've got a very concrete case that I'd like to give you, and please tell me as a demographer how you would have dealt with this particular case in very concrete terms. Let's imagine that in a given village, let's say village X, people in the village learn that the village Y, which is 50 kilometres away, was caught by an armed forces, and that the inhabitants of the village from X, who are 50 kilometres away, decide to leave village X because they think that they may also be subjected to some risks and that there may be some shelling and that they may be caught and captured. Therefore, these people leave village X. Now, the demographer who might look at this situation from the point of view of forcible migration, now, do you think that the inhabitants of village X would be count as forced migrants; or would they be considered as voluntary migrants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a very complex question as far as I'm concerned, because we know who forced -- the forcible migrants are. There's a definition. It's either a refugee or a displaced person who was forced to move out. But if I were to answer to your question the way I understand it, it is very important to know how long these people remained elsewhere, whether they fled for just one, three, or five days, and then went back. If they fled because of some fear, it was their personal motivation. They were motivate by their fear to leave. So the direct answer to your question would require me to know some other elements, whether it lasted for a longer time, whether the fear was justified. Probably, well, all fears in war are justified. Whether those people were able to go back at one point or whether they all remained as internally displaced persons, well, in order to be able to give you a full answer, I would have to know more facts, because they can be forced to migrate or voluntary. But what is important to know is whether, stricto senso, forcible migrants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So, in my case, it's complex question, and a demographer would really have a hard time answering the question. He or she would have to look carefully into all the circumstances in order to make his conclusion. Is that what I'm supposed to deduce from your answer, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, in particular if a demographer has in front of them the OSCE instruction, saying that both voluntary and forcibly displaced persons are displaced persons. The OSCE takes into account that there were situations where somebody may have left their home voluntarily. So not all migrations are classed as forcible migrations, and this is done when voters are registered. A demographer must be aware of the complexity of the situation and must be aware of the definitions of various phenomena and events that they are dealing with and studying them; in particular, when comparisons are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Over to you, Madam West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I'd to look at -- I'd like to look at P 10727, P 10727. It's page 29 of the English and page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will I see it in front of me on the screen? That's easier that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Professor, have you heard of Jean Paul Sardon? He's the French demographer who testified for Serbia in the ICJ case when Bosnia sued Serbia for genocide. Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him. I'm not familiar with his work.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to read a portion of his testimony from the ICJ, and then ask you a question. It's entitled "The Victims of the War in Bosnia-Herzegovina." It's under number 1. It says: "Estimating the number of victims for this conflict is a matter so sensitive and so emblematic of the inter-ethnic conflicts that accompanied the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, that it is more often treated emotionally and as a topic calling for rigorous scientific examination. "All sorts of figures are circulating, selected according to the sensibilities of those who cite them, without their feeling it necessary to test their validity or even simply check their source." Then there's a table of a number of sources and some numbers. And after that, he testified that: "Thus, we have seen the estimates of the number of persons killed and missing blossom, ranging from 20.000 to 328.000, a quite extraordinary ratio of 1 to 16. Most of these estimates circulate without anyone knowing exactly what their sources are or on what basis they were calculated - assuming that they were not the result of some form of spontaneous generation. "The first observation that can be made on analysing these estimates is that their level depends to a large extent on the ..." --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that portion now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You have it in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "The first observation that can be made on analysing these estimates is that their level depends on to a large extent on the geographical origins of their authors. Estimates made in Bosnia-Herzegovina are always much higher than those from outside the country. The average of the local estimates is in excess of 247.000 as against less than half that figure, 118.000, for the average of the foreign estimates. This is relatively common in situations of this type: The victims' side always overestimates its losses. In addition, most of the local figures take into account the increase in the death rate due to the deterioration in living conditions during the war. "Unfortunately, whether the figures were produced inside or outside the former Yugoslavia, it is not at all easy to see how their authors reached them. This is not generally stated at the time of the publication; however, there is a limited number of methods that can be employed: "Using debt statistics supplied by the Sarajevo institute of public health. "Comparing the expected population inherited from the last census, 1991, and the estimated current population. "Combining these two methods."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The next page on the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "The main problem in such work is the lack of critical appraisal of the quality of the sources used, in particular the death-rate data generated by the Institute of Public Health. We know that these greatly overestimated the number of deaths due to double counting. "Among all the estimates to which we have had access, one is conspicuous for its quality, and that prepared -- that is prepared by Ewa Tabeau and Jakub Bijak, demographers attached to the office of the ICTY Prosecutor." Professor, my question is that: Although you have a poor opinion of the report in this case, do you concede that qualified experts in the field would disagree with your assessment of Ewa Tabeau's work?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot agree to a question that is phrased in this manner. I do not agree with Dr. Tabeau's work in terms of the reports that she submitted. Now, as for the assessment for the overall number of victims, she gave an interview in our papers where she denies that The Hague Tribunal actually established this figure at 200.000, 300.000. She provided an estimate. Well, she has lots of data sources, and I think that her estimate is the most realistic one. Now, when it comes to her expert reports --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go back to my question, and my question --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I probably did not understand your question. Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you concede that qualified experts in this field would disagree with your assessment of her work? The answer to that question is a yes or no. Do you concede that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't. I have to say, if you will -- I have to say why I don't concede.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question was does she concede. She does not. That's fine. The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can do redirect. I can do redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps you would be so kind, Professor, to provide a fuller answer to the question posed. So go ahead. I know the Prosecution is not interested in the answer, but we are.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this is not my evaluation of the work of Dr. Tabeau, the overall work that Dr. Tabeau did. This is about the evaluation that the most objective evaluation was given by Dr. Tabeau. In other words, the Prosecution in asking me whether the gentleman who evaluated the work of Dr. Tabeau, and the answer is no. However, he says that her estimates, amongst all the estimates that he lists, are probably the most correct one, and I agree with that. These estimates are probably the most correct ones. I did not deal with the estimates. However, I'm not saying this is the evaluation of the work of Dr. Tabeau. Maybe one particle, maybe one tiny part of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have a few more questions to ask you. You were asked a question as far as how you were able to -- whether you had examined the book from the hospital, the hospital books. You said, Yes, and then you wanted to show how you went about in examining the records. You were reaching for something, and then you were cut off. Again, we are interested to see how exactly you examined those records. Could you please show us?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say this: I was asked to look at the data sources, to evaluate these data sources that may or may not be use by a demographer. I would like to show you how a data source looks like and what served to come up with all the figures and causes of this. I have a page from a death registry in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could be so kind as to explain what this -- where this document is from. We'll have to give it an IC number at some point. So where is this from, and then please proceed by explaining it to us.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This originates from the book of the Mostar War Hospital, which I took from the demographic department of the OTP. This is just one page, and that book has quite a few pages. There are a lot of problems because some pages are missing and so on and so forth. I brought this as an example. As I was looking at this, I was making my decisions about the value and the reliability of this source of data. If you pay attention, you will see that we're dealing with the names and family names of people who were admitted to the hospital, that only their name and last name and the year of birth is entered, and some are also characterised as soldiers and others as civilians. Then there are also diagnosis that the attending physician entered. I am not a doctor, obviously. I'm not a physician. Although I tried to translate some of the diagnoses, I found it difficult. Whether these diagnoses are also the causes of death according to Dr. Tabeau, I don't know. She distributes her data according to the causes of death. I'm sure that she had a doctor's assistance, but I wouldn't know. What I'm trying to say is this: Even good experts, physicians, would have a hard time interpreting these Latin diagnoses. I believe that if you -- if you are considering the causes of death, then you have to list that you were assist by a physician or you have a certificate of death. Second of all, there are a lot of empty columns under the title "Diagnosis." For example, here, there is nothing here. Nothing has been entered under the title "Diagnosis" next to this name. However, there's also -- I apologise. There's also the year of birth missing. You only have the name. So on its own, this document is a very contestable source of data. It really makes you decide to choose only the cases that you really can prove are reliable. In her report, Dr. Tabeau mentions a number of others. She says a number of pages misses. She says pages from 190 to 215 are missing. However, since she assumed that these pages also contained wounded, she also calculates how many persons could be on the missing pages, and she adds them to the total number of wounded that she found on the pages that are there, those who are wounded and those who died of their wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is this an acceptable scientific method recognised within the field of demography?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An expert demographer has to arrange, that's his duty, to arrange his source of data in order to obtain at least a minimally reliable result. Dr. Tabeau does not evaluate this data source as an acceptable, but, rather, says that it is ridden with problems, but I still accept it acceptable. I don't agree with her. I don't know what is the degree of reliability that she attaches to it, if you take into account there are pages missing, if you don't say, or at least you don't say in the report, who was it who interpreted the diagnosis for you, the diagnosis that you claim with the clauses ever death. I don't understand anything about these diagnosis. They may be lethal, they may not be lethal, but I don't know. I would need an expert to help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I have two or three more questions. One had to do with the census. As I understand it from your testimony on direct examination, there was optical scanning done, and that's how it was all computerised, of all the forms that were filled out from the fieldwork; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Optical scanning was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe that you said that Bosnia-Herzegovina was one of the republics that actually had the names that were scanned along with the forms.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw this here in The Hague actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether the instructions given to those who went out in the field to actually fill out the names and the forms --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I haven't finished the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I think it's -- well, excuse me. Please finish the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether in filling out those forms, there were any particular instructions on whether they should use Cyrillic, or the Latin script, to use capital letters? Were there any instructions so you have a uniform approach?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is beyond the scope of the cross. We didn't discuss the optical scanning or the Latin script at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The fact that she didn't mention optical scanning doesn't mean that it is beyond the scope. There were lots of questions with regard to the names and to the changing of the names, and how the demographic department of the OTP took it upon themselves to change names. So it is well within the scope, especially considering that at some point there was further discussion as far as the OTP experts deciding on the basis of names one's particular ethnicity. So I think it's well within the scope, Your Honours, if I could get a ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were two letters, the Latinic script or the Cyrillic scripts. Both could be used equally. There was no recommendation as to what you could use. There was just one recommendation. There were little boxes, and just one letter could be entered in one box.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were they required to use capital letters? Were they required to use capital letters, or could they write in the forms however they wished?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no recommendation. I find this a rather strange question. Nobody actually provided you with a recommendation as to how you should write. You could use any script. You were not supposed to enter two letters in one box. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, based on the optical scanning, were then the names typed on a particular roll, or was it just left to the scanning as far as to the records?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were left in their original form as they were scanned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And afterwards, they were not typed in any way to make a list of who was -- who was on the census, as far as the names were concerned?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You never do that in statistics. A name is not statistical information. In statistical terms, nobody is interested in names. In Serbia, for example, nobody even entered either the first or the last names; Montenegro also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't guarantee about Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether all the names were legible and all the names were correctly spelled when they were optically scanned? That's the essence of my question.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the original material, there were a lot of mistakes. Some were legible, some not. Some had signs instead of proper letters. There were a lot of mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how were those mistakes corrected, if you know? How was a determination made that the -- to make sure that all the names were correctly spelled?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the OTP's experts wrote, it was done with the help of experts for the names of the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But my question was: Was it ever done officially in 1991? That's what my question is.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to statistical bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the case, I repeat, nobody ever controlled, corrected, or was at all interested in the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go on -- well, let me just go back to the OTP. As I understand your previous answer, the OTP did through their experts make attempts or did, in fact, try to figure out the correct names. Do you know whether this is an acceptable practice within demographics; and, if so, are there any particular standards?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of any such thing. I can't even believe that there are standards, how to correct a wrongly written name. I don't even believe that there is a methodology for checking whether the name was entered correctly, unless you went out and collected all of the ID documents and compared them with what you have in your statistical books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether at least the OTP made a list of all the names that they thought were found to be questionable and corrected? So where at least we have a list of those names that we can sort of separate from ones that were known versus the ones that needed to be corrected, did you find such a list by them?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know if the OTP, indeed, has such a list or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, going to your -- one of the issues, it would appear on cross-examination from your answers, was you took exception to the quality control, if I could use that term, in a sense with the matching. You were shown, for instance, Mirsad Halilovic I think was the name, and shown that there was 89.9 per cent matching. Then, as part of your answer, you indicated that while some numbers, some of the JMBG numbers, could be matched, other keys were used for other names in order to do matching. In other words, where numbers were not available, other keys were used. Do I have your testimony correct, if I ask my next question?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you understood me correctly. If there is no JMBG, what was used were names and last names. But we don't know if anything at all was done with regard to the JMBG, so I really am not in a position to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me go step-by-step. It usually helps. In addition to -- I should say, aside from the ones that they were able to match with the JMBG numbers, did the OTP keep records, so you can make a determination as to how they did the other matching, who was matched by other procedures other than the JMBG, so then you could look at those names and see whether the matching was done correctly?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the answer would be no. There's no single report with a reference to something of that sort having been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand your testimony, you indicated that in order to augment the numbers, they kept changing the key in order to get more matches, to create more matches, to augment the numbers; is that correct. Do I understand your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in this case, in order to augment the numbers. There are also cases when the numbers were reduced. It all depended on what they wanted to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, specifically with respect to the keys, the different keys that were used in order to make the different sorts of matching, is there anywhere in their records that you can look at as a demographer and you can say 30 per cent or 40 per cent were matched by simply looking at the JMBG numbers; 20 per cent were matched by this other method, only data of births; 10 per cent were match in some other fashion? Is there anything of that sort for you then as a demographer to look at and examine so you would know exactly how they arrived at a particular number, at the final result?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA RADOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reference to that matching statistics in any of the reports that I've had an occasion to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.
